prize_parts.citation: For showing how collateral constraints link credit limits to asset prices, so that small shocks are amplified and propagated into persistent macroeconomic fluctuations.

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed from B015 to B004 with Kiyotaki and Moore, for reasons of attribution and not because I now think B015 is less important. Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) is a single, identifiable discovery. A durable, collateralisable asset ties borrowing limits to asset prices, and the feedback turns temporary shocks into persistent downturns. It has had about three decades of extension and use, including the 2007-09 crisis, so maturity is not in question. The two-name credit is the cleanest of any shortlisted configuration. Several colleagues from different fields converge on the same core: Andersson and Strömberg as supporters, and Boppart and Enflo as alternative-listers. Support counts are not scientific merit. What I rely on is that the three-name cap does not force an arbitrary cut here. In round 1 I defended the Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio as the originators of building blocks, but I also conceded that Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler have strong claims and that Calvo-style pricing fits micro price data only partly. After the exchange I weigh that attribution cost more heavily than I did before. I am keeping the citation to the collateral-constraint mechanism. I am not claiming the whole financial-accelerator strand, so the award does not overstate what the pair did.
statement.case_against: The main weakness is marginal novelty. The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises covers adjacent ground, and a committee could see a financial-frictions award so soon afterwards as a repeat. I think the mechanism is distinct from the bank-run and intermediation work and from the Bernanke accelerator, but this is a judgement. A pair also leaves out Gertler's work on financial intermediaries with Kiyotaki, and Gilchrist's empirical work. Strömberg and Andersson argue that this intermediary strand is what brought the mechanism into post-2008 policy models. The aggregate evidence for the mechanism is mostly indirect or calibrated, not cleanly identified. B002 has the broadest opening support and a plausible case on merit. B015 remains the more consequential framework for policy practice, and my doubts there are about who to credit, not about the science. I rely on general knowledge, not on independent verification of citations.

responses.point: Strömberg keeps Gertler in the B004 trio for his later work with Kiyotaki on intermediary balance sheets. He says a Kiyotaki-Moore pair is a defensible fallback if the 2022 prize is judged to have exhausted the accelerator territory, and that the choice should rest on the attribution argument and not on a wish for a smaller prize.
responses.response: I take that condition seriously and my answer is on attribution. The Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is a self-contained discovery, and the citation I propose is about that mechanism and nothing wider. Gertler's intermediary work extends it, and I think it is a real contribution. I am not convinced it is the same discovery, because it is joined to the accelerator and New Keynesian strands that he also appears in. Crediting him here brings back the diffusion problem that made me doubt B015. I would not call a trio indefensible, and if the committee finds the intermediary strand separable I could support it. I still prefer the pair because it is the only version where each credited name is clearly part of one discovery. I accept your point that the choice must be argued and not assumed.

responses.point: Andersson prefers B004 with Gertler but says Kiyotaki and Moore are indispensable and that the pair is the cleanest fallback. He also treats the mechanism's absorption into crisis analysis as evidence of lasting importance and not of redundancy with 2022.
responses.response: I agree with the absorption argument and it is a large part of why I moved. A mechanism that became a standard tool in crisis analysis has shown more durability than a candidate that is only influential. We differ a little on Gertler. You see his inclusion as the main point you hold less firmly, and I read your concession as support for the pair. On B015 you ranked it eighth because of attribution. In round 1 I wrote that this was a real cost and that I could not fully answer it. I now think the force of that objection is larger than I allowed. Our remaining difference is about the third name, not about the science.

responses.point: Teorell accepts that B015 is of very high importance, which he ranks third, but says attribution is the problem. Any three names leave out Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler, and the framework was built cumulatively. He says B027 has a tighter joint core.
responses.response: I agree with the diagnosis and it applies to my own first choice. I argued that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are originators of building blocks and that the others are developers. I now doubt that this criterion can be applied without argument over each name, and Krusell's reply did not remove that doubt for me. I do not extend the same conclusion to B027. I see its pair-versus-trio question as comparable to B004's, and both reduce to a cleaner pair. The 2024 prize makes me more cautious about B027 on timing than on science. So on this point we agree on B015, and the comparison between B004 and B027 turns for me on identification of the mechanism and on proximity to recent prizes, which both of us admit cuts both ways.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B002 first. He says B015's attribution is weaker than B002's, that a Kiyotaki-Moore core is the cleanest attribution for B004, and that he would accept the narrower option. He also treats B002's long-run causal claims as still being tested.
responses.response: Your attribution comparison is the main reason I moved, and I thank you for putting it plainly. B002 and B004 differ on the other criterion, maturity. B004 has a three-decade record that includes a very large test in 2008. B002's core results are from 2014-2022, and you and I both note that the causal reading of place effects is still contested. I do not say B002 is unworthy. In round 1 I said I would not oppose it in a later year, and a citation limited to measurement and exposure-based designs would address much of my worry. Where I differ is on how much to weight a shorter record when a mature and cleanly attributed alternative exists. I should also disclose that my own work on social mobility makes me a poor judge of B002's novelty.

responses.point: Krusell keeps B015 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He argues that each is the originator of a distinct building block, that post-2021 inflation questions medium-scale forecasting and not the pricing or policy-rule logic, and that his agreement with me should not count as independent corroboration.
responses.response: I agree that the post-2021 debate does not by itself undermine the rule logic or the welfare framework, and I still think the contribution is foundational. I also agree that our agreement in round 1 should not have counted as independent evidence, and I note that I am now moving away from it. The change comes from the attribution cost you also concede, that this is the one candidate where the cap may do real injustice to colleagues. A prize should not rest on a split that I and several members cannot defend case by case. I regard B015 as a serious alternative and I will not hide that. If the committee comes to an agreed originators criterion, which the chair's questions ask for, I would reconsider.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises as having covered the collateral-constraint mechanism, or whether Kiyotaki-Moore is a separate discovery with its own claim.
Whether a pair is better than a trio with Gertler. This turns on whether the intermediary-finance strand is separable from the Bernanke accelerator and from Gertler's role in B015.
Whether indirect or calibrated aggregate evidence should count against a mechanism whose firm- and household-level support is cumulative.

Whether my move from B015 is an overcorrection. The eight-name credit problem is real, but a committee that finds an agreed originators criterion could make B015 the stronger choice on scientific consequence.
Whether B002's long-run causal place-effect claims will mature enough to change the comparison with B004, for example through replication in non-US administrative data.
My assessments rest on general knowledge of the literature and the supplied round-1 files and have not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. The supplied profile lists Per Krusell (secretary) as a frequent co-author and IIES colleague, and he prefers B015, which I no longer prefer. I co-authored a menu-costs paper with Richard Friberg and a paper with Timo Boppart. My own social-mobility research is adjacent to B002, an alternative. My profile lists no co-authorship or institutional connection with Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler, Gilchrist, Calvo, Taylor or Woodford. My 2018 presentation speech and the 2018 background citing Golosov, Hassler, Krusell and Tsyvinski (2014) concern climate economics and not any shortlisted entry. I am chair and wrote the round-1 summary, so I have tried to treat my own preference as one view among eleven. These are disclosures, not recusal adjudications.
